ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY

40 CFR Part 52

[EPA-R09-OAR-2026-5119; FRL-13482-01-R9]


Approval and Promulgation of Implementation Plans--Pinal County 
(Part); West Pinal, AZ PM10 Nonattainment Area; Moderate Area, Serious 
Area, and Section 189(d) Plan for Attainment of the 24-Hour PM10 
Standard

AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

ACTION: Proposed rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to 
approve a state implementation plan (SIP) revision submitted by the 
State of Arizona to meet Clean Air Act (CAA or ``Act'') requirements 
applicable to the Pinal County (Part); West Pinal PM10 
nonattainment area (``West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment 
Area''). The EPA is proposing to find that the submitted SIP revision 
meets all applicable ``Moderate'' area, ``Serious'' area, and CAA 
section 189(d) requirements for the PM10 national ambient 
air quality standards (NAAQS). Additionally, the EPA is proposing to 
approve the PM10 motor vehicle emissions budgets included 
with the SIP revision for transportation conformity purposes. The EPA 
is also starting the adequacy process for these budgets. Our proposed 
approval of the SIP revision would establish an attainment date of 
December 31, 2026, for the area.

DATES: Comments must be received on or before November 18, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-R09-
OAR-2026-5119 at https://www.regulations.gov. For comments submitted at 
Regulations.gov, follow the online instructions for submitting 
comments. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from 
Regulations.gov. The EPA may publish any comment received to its public 
docket. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be 
Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose 
disclosure is restricted by statute. Multimedia submissions (audio, 
video, etc.) must be accompanied by a written comment.

I. Executive Summary

A. What proposed action is the EPA taking?

    The EPA is proposing to approve a SIP revision submitted by the 
State of Arizona to meet all Moderate area, Serious area, and CAA 
section 189(d) requirements applicable to the West Pinal County 
PM10 Nonattainment Area for the PM10 NAAQS. The 
EPA is also proposing to approve the PM10 motor vehicle 
emissions budgets included with the SIP revision for transportation 
conformity purposes and is starting the adequacy process for these 
budgets.

B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?

    CAA sections 188 and 189 contain specific planning and control 
requirements relevant to the PM10 NAAQS while CAA sections 
110 and 172 contain general planning and control requirements for all 
nonattainment plans.
    The EPA is proposing approval of the baseline and attainment year 
emission inventory requirements of CAA section 172(c)(3), the BACM 
demonstration requirements of CAA section 189(b)(1)(B), the RACM 
demonstration requirements of CAA sections 189(a)(1)(C) and 172(c)(1), 
the attainment demonstration requirements of CAA sections 189(d) and 
179(d)(3), the five percent demonstration requirements of CAA section 
189(d), the reasonable further progress and quantitative milestone 
demonstration requirements of CAA sections 172(c)(2) and 189(c), the 
contingency measures requirements of CAA section 172(c)(9), and the 
motor vehicle emissions budgets as meeting the criteria for budgets in 
CAA section 176(c) and 40 CFR 93.118(e). The EPA is also starting the 
adequacy process for these budgets under 40 CFR 93.188(f).

II. PM10 Air Quality Planning in the West Pinal County PM10 
Nonattainment Area

    The NAAQS are standards for certain ambient air pollutants set by 
the EPA to protect public health and welfare. Particulate matter with a 
diameter of ten microns or less (PM10) is among the ambient 
air pollutants for which the EPA has established health-based 
standards. PM10 causes adverse health effects by penetrating 
deep in the lungs, aggravating the cardiopulmonary system. Children, 
the elderly, and people with asthma and heart conditions are the most 
vulnerable.
    On July 1, 1987, the EPA revised the health-based NAAQS for 
particulate matter, establishing two PM10 standards, an 
annual standard and a 24-hour standard.\1\ Effective December 18, 2006, 
the EPA revoked the annual PM10 standard but retained the 
24-hour PM10 standard.\2\ The 24-hour PM10 
standard of 150 micrograms per cubic meter ([micro]g/m\3\) is attained 
when the expected number of days with a 24-hour average concentration 
above 150 [micro]g/m\3\ per calendar year averaged over a three-year 
period, as determined in accordance with appendix K to 40 CFR part 50, 
is equal to or less than one.\3\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ 52 FR 24672 (July 1, 1987).
    \2\ 71 FR 61144 (Oct. 17, 2006).
    \3\ 40 CFR 50.6 and 40 CFR part 50, appendix K.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    On May 31, 2012, the EPA designated a portion of State lands in 
Pinal County, Arizona (``West Pinal County'') as nonattainment for the 
1987 PM10 NAAQS based on 2006-2008 data.\4\ West Pinal 
County is located in central Arizona, southeast of the Phoenix 
metropolitan area and northwest of the city of Tucson. Pinal County 
covers 5,365 square miles and has two distinct western and eastern 
regions with

[[Page 66050]]

different characteristics relevant to pollution formation. The West 
Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area is located within the 
western region, characterized by low desert valleys and an arid 
climate. The eastern region is mountainous, with elevations up to 6,441 
feet. The West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area 
encompasses all land geographically located within Pinal County west of 
the north-south line defined by the boundary between Townships 10E and 
11E, but excluding the main reservation of the Tohono O'odham Nation 
and excluding the Apache Junction portion of the existing Phoenix 
PM10 nonattainment area.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \4\ 77 FR 32024 (May 31, 2012). The boundaries for the West 
Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area are described in 40 
CFR 81.303.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As a result of the nonattainment designation, the West Pinal County 
PM10 Nonattainment Area was classified as a Moderate 
PM10 nonattainment area with an attainment date of as 
expeditiously as practicable, but no later than December 31, 2018. The 
Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ) submitted a SIP 
revision intended to meet the Moderate PM10 nonattainment 
requirements on December 21, 2015 (``2015 West Pinal Plan'').
    On June 24, 2020, the EPA determined that West Pinal County 
PM10 Nonattainment Area did not attain the 1987 
PM10 NAAQS by December 31, 2018.\5\ Pursuant to CAA section 
188(b)(2), the area was reclassified to ``Serious'' nonattainment with 
an attainment date of as expeditiously as practicable, but no later 
than December 31, 2022.\6\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ 85 FR 37756 (June 24, 2020).

III. Overview of Applicable CAA Requirements

    As a Serious PM10 nonattainment area that failed to 
attain the NAAQS by its applicable attainment date of December 31, 
2022, the West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area is 
subject to the requirements of CAA section 189(d). In addition, because 
the EPA has not previously approved a Moderate or a Serious area plan 
for the West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area, the area 
is also required to demonstrate that it has met the requirements 
associated with these classifications.
    CAA section 189(d) provides that the State shall ``submit within 12 
months after the applicable attainment date, plan revisions that 
provide for attainment of the PM10 air quality standard and, 
from the date of such submission until attainment, for an annual 
reduction of PM10 or PM10 precursor emissions 
within the area of not less than 5 percent of the amount of such 
emissions as reported in the most recent inventory prepared for the 
area.''
    The general planning and control requirements for all nonattainment 
plans are found in CAA sections 110 and 172. More specific planning and 
control requirements relevant to the PM10 NAAQS are found in 
part D, subpart 4, in CAA sections 188 and 189. The EPA has issued a 
General Preamble \17\ and Addendum to the General Preamble \18\ to 
provide guidance to States for meeting the CAA's requirements for the 
PM10 NAAQS. The General Preamble mainly addresses the 
requirements for Moderate nonattainment areas and the Addendum 
addresses the requirements for Serious nonattainment areas. The EPA has 
also issued other guidance documents

[[Page 66051]]

related to PM10 plans that are discussed and cited below. 
The specific PM10 attainment planning requirements addressed 
by this SIP submission are summarized below.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \17\ ``State Implementation Plans; General Preamble for the 
Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990,'' 
57 FR 13498 (Apr. 16, 1992) (``General Preamble'') and 57 FR 18070 
(Apr. 28, 1992).
    \18\ ``State Implementation Plans for Serious PM-10 
Nonattainment Areas, and Attainment Date Waivers for PM-10 
Nonattainment Areas Generally; Addendum to the General Preamble for 
the Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 
1990,'' 59 FR 41998 (Aug. 16, 1994) (``Addendum'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Emissions Inventories

    CAA section 172(c)(3) requires a ``base year inventory'' that is a 
comprehensive, accurate, current inventory of actual emissions from all 
sources of the relevant pollutant or pollutants in the area. The plan 
should also include a second projected attainment year inventory for 
the year that the area is projected to attain the PM10 
standards.

B. PM10 Precursors

    CAA section 189(e) requires that the control requirements for major 
stationary sources of direct PM10 also apply to major 
stationary sources of PM10 precursors, except where the 
Administrator determines that such sources do not contribute 
significantly to PM10 levels that exceed the standard in the 
area. While CAA section 189(e) expressly requires control of precursors 
from major stationary sources, subpart 4 and other CAA provisions 
collectively require the control of direct PM10 and 
PM10 precursors from all types of sources (i.e., stationary 
sources, area sources and mobile sources) as may be needed for the 
purposes of demonstrating attainment as expeditiously as practicable in 
a given nonattainment area.\19\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \19\ See CAA requirements for States to demonstrate attainment 
``as expeditiously as practicable,'' CAA sections 188(c)(1) and 
172(a)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

C. Best Available Control Measures and Reasonably Available Control 
Measures Demonstration

    CAA section 189(b)(1)(B) requires that Serious area PM10 
attainment plans provide for the implementation of best available 
control measures (BACM) within four years of reclassification to 
Serious. Because the Serious area attainment date of December 31, 2022, 
has passed, and the EPA found that the area failed to attain by the 
Serious area attainment date,\20\ we are evaluating the submission for 
compliance with the BACM requirements now, in conjunction with the 
State's SIP submission intended to meet the Moderate area, Serious 
area, and CAA section 189(d) plan requirements. Furthermore, because 
the EPA has not previously taken action to approve the SIP as meeting 
the subpart 4 reasonably available control measures (RACM) Moderate 
area planning requirements under CAA section 189 for the West Pinal 
County PM10 Nonattainment Area, the EPA is reviewing the 
2023 Five Percent Plan for compliance with those requirements as 
well.\21\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \20\ See note 13.
    \21\ The EPA does not normally conduct a separate evaluation to 
determine whether a Serious area plan's measures also meet the RACM 
requirements. As explained in the Addendum to the General Preamble, 
we interpret the BACM requirement as generally subsuming the RACM 
requirement--i.e., if we determine that the measures are indeed the 
``best available,'' we have necessarily concluded that they are 
``reasonably available.'' (Addendum to the General Preamble, 42010). 
Therefore, a separate analysis to determine if the measures 
represent a RACM level of control is not necessary. A proposed 
approval of a Plan's provisions concerning implementation of BACM is 
also a proposed finding that the Plan provides for the 
implementation of RACM.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

D. CAA Section 189(d) Attainment Demonstration and Five Percent 
Requirement

    For Serious PM10 nonattainment areas that do not attain 
the PM10 NAAQS by the applicable attainment date, CAA 
section 189(d) requires the State to submit plan revisions that provide 
for attainment of the NAAQS (i.e., an attainment demonstration) as 
expeditiously as practicable, but no later than five years from the 
publication date of the notice of a nonattainment finding. The plan 
must also provide for an annual five percent reduction in 
PM10 or PM10 precursor emissions for each year 
from the date of submission until attainment. CAA section 189(d) 
specifies that the State must submit these plan revisions within 12 
months of the applicable attainment date that the area failed to meet.

E. Reasonable Further Progress and Quantitative Milestones

    CAA section 172(c)(2) requires that implementation plans 
demonstrate reasonable further progress (RFP) as defined in CAA section 
171(1). CAA section 171(1) defines RFP as ``such annual incremental 
reductions in emissions of the relevant air pollutant as are required 
by this part [part D of title I] or may reasonably be required by the 
Administrator for the purpose of ensuring attainment of the applicable 
national ambient air quality standard by the applicable date.'' The 
general RFP requirement of CAA section 172(c)(2) applies to SIP 
submissions necessary to meet CAA section 189(d) for the 
PM10 NAAQS.
    In addition, CAA section 189(c)(1), specifically applicable to the 
PM10 NAAQS, requires that an implementation plan contain 
quantitative milestones that will be achieved every three years and 
that will demonstrate that RFP is being met.

F. Contingency Measures

    CAA section 172(c)(9) requires that implementation plans provide 
for ``the implementation of specific measures to be undertaken if the 
area fails to make reasonable further progress, or to attain the NAAQS 
by the attainment date applicable under this part [part D of title I]. 
Such measures are to take effect in any such case without further 
action by the State or the Administrator.'' The contingency measure 
requirement of CAA section 172(c)(9) applies to the SIP submissions 
necessary to meet CAA section 189(d) for the PM10 NAAQS.

G. Transportation Conformity and Motor Vehicle Emissions Budgets

    Transportation conformity is required by CAA section 176(c). The 
conformity regulations found at 40 CFR part 93, subpart A require that 
transportation plans, programs, and projects conform to the purpose of 
the SIP and establish the criteria and procedures for determining 
whether or not they do so. Conformity to the purpose of the SIP means 
that transportation activities will not produce new air quality 
violations, worsen existing violations, or delay timely attainment of 
the NAAQS or any interim milestones. Once a SIP that contains motor 
vehicle emissions budgets (``budgets'') has been submitted to the EPA, 
and the Agency has found them adequate, these budgets are used for 
determining conformity: emissions from planned transportation 
activities must be less than or equal to the budgets.\22\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \22\ See 40 CFR 93.118(a) to (e).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

H. Adequate Authority

    CAA section 110(a)(2)(E)(i) requires that implementation plans 
provide necessary assurances that the State (or the general purpose 
local government or regional agency designated by the State for this 
purpose) will have adequate personnel, funding and authority under 
State law to carry out the requirements of such plan. Requirements for 
legal authority are further defined in 40 CFR part 51, subpart L 
(51.230-51.232) and for resources in 40 CFR 51.280. States and 
responsible local agencies must also demonstrate that they have the 
legal authority to adopt and enforce provisions of the SIP and to 
obtain information necessary to determine compliance.

[[Page 66052]]

IV. Evaluation of the 2023 Five Percent Plan's Compliance With CAA 
Requirements

A. Emissions Inventories

    CAA section 172(c)(3) requires all nonattainment area plans to 
include a base year emissions inventory that is a comprehensive, 
accurate, and current inventory of actual emissions from all sources of 
the relevant pollutant or pollutants in the area at issue. Also, the 
State should submit a projected attainment year emissions inventory for 
the year in which the State projects that the area will attain the 
PM10 standards. The EPA's emission inventory guidance 
provides recommendations on how to develop and document emission 
inventories.\23\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \23\ See ``Emissions Inventory Guidance for Implementation of 
Ozone and Particulate Matter National Ambient Air Quality Standards 
(NAAQS) and Regional Haze Regulations,'' EPA, May 2017 (``2017 EI 
Guidance'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The 2023 Five Percent Plan uses a 2017 base year emissions 
inventory for Pinal County (``2017 PM10 Inventory'') as a 
starting point in the analysis. The 2017 PM10 Inventory was 
developed by ADEQ, Pinal County Air Quality Control District (PCAQCD), 
and MAG. The 2017 PM10 Inventory included emissions from 
point sources (permitted sources), nonpoint sources (area sources), 
nonroad mobile sources, and on-road mobile sources. This emission 
inventory is sufficiently comprehensive, covering all sources of 
PM10 that have been found to be important sources of 
relevant emissions in this and other PM10 nonattainment 
areas.
    The 2017 PM10 Inventory shows that the most significant 
sources of annual emissions in the West Pinal County PM10 
Nonattainment Area are unpaved road dust: private roads (31.5 percent), 
unpaved road dust: agricultural roads (24.7 percent), unpaved road 
dust: public roads (16.2 percent), windblown dust (9.0 percent), 
tilling and harvesting (5.0 percent), feedlots (3.3 percent), and 
construction (2.7 percent). The annual and daily PM10 
emissions inventories and the emission estimation methodologies used to 
develop the 2017 PM10 Inventory are described in detail in 
Appendix A, Exhibit 1 of the 2023 Five Percent Plan.
    In general, the base year emissions inventory represents the 
emissions contributing to the air quality problem addressed by the SIP 
revision. Because the EPA's final rule determining that the West Pinal 
County PM10 Nonattainment Area failed to attain the 
PM10 standard by its attainment date used 2020-2022 
monitoring data to make its determination, a year that is included 
within that time period and the triennial schedule of the National 
Emission Inventory (NEI) would generally be an appropriate base year. 
While the 2020 NEI year would have been the most recent such year to 
consider at the time of this plan's development, due to COVID-related 
emissions anomalies, the 2023 Five Percent Plan concludes that 2020 was 
not an appropriate inventory year. The base year, 2017, was chosen as 
it is a reasonably current NEI year, and the most recent NEI year 
available that was not 2020 at the time of plan development.
    The 2017 PM10 Inventory includes only primary 
PM10 emissions and does not include emissions for 
PM10 precursors. As described in section IV.B of this 
document, MAG determined that precursors do not play a significant role 
in the PM10 exceedances in the West Pinal County 
PM10 Nonattainment Area and the EPA's analysis supports this 
conclusion.
    The 2023 Five Percent Plan includes a 2026 projected attainment 
year emissions inventory (``attainment year inventory'') that was 
developed using annual PM10 emissions under implementation 
of Moderate area (existing) controls from the 2017 base year inventory 
through 2021 and Serious area controls from 2022 through 2026. Emission 
growth factors were developed for each source category relative to 2017 
(growth or decline) and applied based on factors including, but not 
limited to, forecasted total population growth and vehicle miles 
traveled (VMT). Control reductions were then applied as appropriate, 
based on category-specific control effectiveness estimates for each 
individual measure. The resulting 2026 attainment year inventory was 
then provided for each source category and in total.\24\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \24\ 2023 Five Percent Plan, Appendix B, Exhibit I, pp. III-59-
III-62.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In developing the emissions inventories, MAG followed the EPA's 
2017 EI Guidance and recommendations regarding the use of emission 
factors, activity estimates, and control factors, and the other source-
specific inventory development methodologies. The relative accuracy of 
each estimate underwent the prescribed quality assurance procedures, 
documented in the State's emissions inventory preparation plan.\25\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \25\ 2023 Five Percent Plan, ``Pinal County PM Inventory 
Preparation Plan,'' Report No. SR2013-01-01, prepared by Sierra 
Research for the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality, 
February 2013.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The EPA's analysis indicates the inventories are sufficiently 
accurate for the purposes of the 2023 Five Percent Plan. Because we 
find that the inventory is current, comprehensive, and accurate, we 
propose to approve the 2017 PM10 base year inventory and 
2026 attainment year inventory under CAA section 172(c)(3).

B. PM10 Precursors

    The provisions of subpart 4 of part D, title I of the CAA do not 
define the term ``precursor'' for purposes of PM10, nor do 
they explicitly require the control of any specific particulate matter 
(PM) precursor. The statutory definition of ``air pollutant'' in CAA 
section 302(g), however, provides that the term ``includes any 
precursors to the formation of any air pollutant, to the extent the 
Administrator has identified such precursor or precursors for the 
particular purpose for which the term `air pollutant' is used.'' The 
EPA has identified sulfur dioxide (SO2), oxides of nitrogen 
(NOX), volatile organic compounds (VOC), and ammonia 
(NH3) as precursors to the formation of PM.\26\ Accordingly, 
a State must include emissions of direct PM and these four precursors 
in emissions inventories and must control emissions from sources of all 
of these pollutants, unless the State demonstrates to the EPA's 
satisfaction that control of one or more of these pollutants is not 
needed for expeditious attainment of the NAAQS in the nonattainment 
area at issue.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

C. Best Available Control Measures and Reasonably Available Control 
Measures Demonstration

    CAA section 189(b)(1)(B) requires that Serious area PM10 
plans provide for the implementation of BACM within four years of 
reclassification to Serious.\30\ The EPA has established a process for 
evaluating potential BACM (including best available control technology 
(BACT)) in Serious areas.\31\ The first step in determining BACM is to 
develop a comprehensive emissions inventory of the sources of 
PM10 that can be used with modeling to determine the effects 
of these sources on ambient PM10 levels. Based on our review 
of the emission inventories provided in the 2023 Five Percent Plan, the 
EPA's analysis indicates that the 2023 Five Percent Plan appropriately 
identifies all sources of PM10 that are subject to 
evaluation for potential control consistent with the requirements of 
subpart 4 of part D, title I of the Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \30\ As noted in section III.C, because the EPA has not 
previously approved an attainment plan for the Moderate area 
classification, the EPA is also evaluating the submission against 
the RACM requirement.
    \31\ Addendum, 42012.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The remaining steps are to identify potential control measures for 
each source category, determine whether available control measures or 
technologies are technologically and economically feasible for 
implementation in the area, and determine the earliest date by which 
those control measures or technologies found to be feasible can be 
implemented, in whole or in part. In accordance with these steps, the 
significant source categories examined for BACM evaluation in the 2023 
Five Percent Plan are: Construction Sites, Cleared Areas, Dairies, 
Cattle Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations, Agriculture (Cropland), 
Unpaved Roads, Unpaved Lots, and Paved Roads.
    We provide a detailed evaluation of the 2023 Five Percent Plan's 
control measures for sources in the nonattainment area in the EPA's 
``Technical Support Document, EPA Evaluation of BACM, West Pinal County 
2023 Five Percent Plan for the 1987 PM-10 NAAQS,'' July 2026 (``EPA's 
BACM TSD'').\32\ The EPA notes that its BACM analysis is based on the 
rules currently approved in the Pinal County SIP, as well as rules that 
the EPA is proposing to approve elsewhere in today's Federal Register--
specifically, regulations addressing fugitive dust and agricultural 
best management practices. As described in further detail in EPA's BACM 
TSD, we find that the evaluation process followed by MAG in the 2023 
Five Percent Plan to identify potential BACM is consistent with the 
requirements, the evaluation of potential measures is appropriate, and 
reasoned justifications are provided for the rejection of potential 
measures based on technological or economic infeasibility.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \32\ Technical Support Document, EPA Evaluation of BACM, West 
Pinal County 2023 Five Percent Plan for the 1987 PM-10 NAAQS.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For the foregoing reasons, we propose to find that the 2023 Five 
Percent Plan provides for the implementation of BACM for all required 
sources of PM10 in accordance with the requirements of CAA 
section 189(b)(1)(B).
    The EPA does not normally conduct a separate evaluation to 
determine whether a Serious area plan's measures also meet the RACM 
requirements. However, because in this instance, we have not previously 
approved a Moderate area plan as meeting the RACM requirement, we must 
evaluate the control strategy for RACM as well. As explained in the 
General Preamble Addendum, we interpret the BACM requirement as 
generally subsuming the RACM requirement-- i.e., if we determine that 
the measures are indeed the ``best available,'' we have necessarily 
concluded that they are ``reasonably available.'' \33\ Therefore, we 
have not conducted a separate analysis to determine if the measures 
represent a RACM level of control, and propose to find that the 
measures satisfy the RACM requirement, because our analysis indicates 
that they meet the stricter BACM requirement.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \33\ 59 FR 41998, 42010 (Aug. 16, 1994).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

D. CAA Section 189(d) Attainment Demonstration and Five Percent 
Requirement

    CAA section 189(d) requires the submittal of plan revisions that 
provide for expeditious attainment of the PM10 NAAQS. The 
attainment deadline applicable to an area that fails to attain by the 
Serious area attainment date is as soon as practicable, but no later 
than five years from the publication date of the notice of a 
nonattainment finding unless extended by the EPA as meeting certain 
specified requirements.\34\ Because the EPA published the nonattainment 
finding for the West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area on 
July 21, 2023, the State must demonstrate attainment no later than July 
21, 2028, unless the date is extended.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \34\ CAA section 179(d)(3).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Attainment Deadline
    The 2023 Five Percent Plan models attainment of the PM10 
NAAQS by December 31, 2026. The 2023 Five Percent Plan contains a 
demonstration supporting the conclusion that December 31, 2026, is as 
expeditiously as the area can attain the standard. Due to the timeline 
for feasible development and implementation of control measures, the 
first full year that all control measures relied upon in the plan would 
be implemented was 2024. Therefore the 2026 design value, which 
includes 2024-2026 data, is the first design value year to include 
three years of fully implemented control measures. MAG also notes that 
maximum compliance rates will not be achieved until 2026. For these 
reasons, the EPA agrees that the submission shows that the area could 
not practicably attain the NAAQS prior to December 31, 2026.
2. Modeled Attainment Demonstration
    The 2023 Five Percent Plan shows attainment of the PM10 
NAAQS through modeled attainment demonstrations for three sites (Hidden 
Valley, Pinal County Housing, and Stanfield) in the West Pinal County 
PM10 Nonattainment Area.\35\ MAG conducted modeling for 
seven design days across the three monitoring sites, representing the 
meteorological conditions associated with exceedances in the 
nonattainment area.\36\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35\ The Plan also contains an unmonitored area analysis for the 
region surrounding the Hidden Valley monitor.
    \36\ Exceedances of the PM10 NAAQS have been 
associated with three general meteorological scenarios: low wind/
stagnant conditions, elevated wind conditions, and high wind dust 
events. MAG selected design days that would likely not be considered 
high wind dust events (i.e., the geographic extent of the 
exceedances did not suggest the occurrence of an area-wide storm 
event, resulting in emissions that could not be reasonably 
controlled).

    The methods used for modeling the design days are consistent with 
EPA guidance.37 38 The results of the modeling demonstrate 
that the emission reductions in the plan are expected to result in 
PM10 levels that provide for attainment of the NAAQS by 
December 31, 2026. The EPA notes that preliminary ambient air quality 
data for the area suggest that the control strategy may not have 
achieved reductions at the levels predicted in the Plan. The EPA has 
not identified deficiencies in the modeling, or in the substantive 
requirements contained in the rules that constitute the control 
strategy that would cause this discrepancy. However, the EPA has 
previously noted that an earlier version of the AgBMP rules, which 
regulate sources that predominate in the area surrounding the design 
value monitor, may not have contained implementation requirements 
sufficient to achieve the level of compliance predicted in the 
Plan.\39\ The State has updated the AgBMP rules, substantially 
strengthening the enforceability of the rules in a manner that the EPA 
expects will result in reductions in line with those modeled in the 
Plan.\40\ Therefore, the EPA proposes to find that the 2023 Five 
Percent Plan's attainment demonstration adequately demonstrates 
attainment of the PM10 standard in the West Pinal County 
PM10 Nonattainment Area. The EPA's detailed analysis of the 
modeling can be found in EPA's Modeling TSD for this action.

3. Five Percent Requirement
    Under CAA section 189(d), the SIP revision submitted by the State 
must provide for an annual reduction in PM10 or 
PM10 precursor emissions of not less than five percent from 
the date of such submission until attainment. The 2023 Five Percent 
Plan's demonstration of annual five percent reductions is found in 
Chapter 6. MAG used the 2017 PM10 Inventory as the baseline 
inventory and derived emissions levels for years 2017-2027 based on the 
2017 PM10 Inventory.\41\ The demonstration of annual five 
percent reductions uses 2024 as the point at which the reductions 
should start.\42\ Since the plan demonstrates attainment by December 
31, 2026, annual five percent reductions are shown for three years: 
2024, 2025, and 2026. The 2023 Five Percent Plan's demonstration is 
summarized in Table 2 of this document.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \41\ 2023 Five Percent Plan, Chapter 6, p. 6-1.
    \42\ Id. The EPA notes that ADEQ submitted the 2023 Five Percent 
Plan on December 14, 2023. Because CAA section 189(d) states that 
the reductions should be shown ``from the date of such submission 
until attainment,'' the Plan should show the five percent reductions 
beginning on that date. However, the EPA finds that showing 
reductions beginning in 2024 is sufficient. First, the amount of 
time between submission and the beginning of the reduction period is 
minimal--less than three weeks. Second, the emission inventories 
used to calculate the reductions are generally on a calendar year 
basis. Accordingly, the EPA believes it was reasonable to wait until 
the turn of the calendar year, given the short amount of time 
between the dates. Third, the submitted analysis shows excess 
reductions that more than account for the small amount of reductions 
that would be required in a small pro-rated portion of 2023 that 
remained at the time of submission. See Table 2 of this document. 
And fourth, the State could have waited until the turn of the year 
to submit the Plan to avoid needing to account for these days in 
late 2023, and the EPA does not agree that it is appropriate to 
provide an incentive for the State to delay plan submittal. The EPA 
has articulated, in the context of the CAA section 189(d) 
requirements for PM2.5, that it is sufficient to show 
reductions from the due date of the CAA section 189(d) plan. The EPA 
has noted that this prevents States making late submissions from 
avoiding the requirement to achieve reductions for the timeframe of 
the delay. See 81 FR 58010, 58101; 86 FR 53150, 53166 (Sep. 24, 
2021).

    The ``2017 Baseline Inventory (tons)'' values are derived from the 
2017 PM10 Inventory. The ``Five Percent Annual Requirement 
(tons)'' values indicate the annual five percent reduction target as

(41,168 tons) by five percent, resulting in a value of 2,058 tons. The 
``Five Percent Cumulative Reduction (tons)'' indicate the cumulative 
yearly

reductions, increasing by five percent of the 2017 Baseline Inventory 
each year.
    The ``2017 Base PM10 Emissions Minus Five Percent Annual 
Reductions (tons)'' values are calculated as the ``2017 Baseline 
Inventory (tons)'' minus the ``Five Percent Annual Requirement 
(tons),'' representing the maximum total emission in tons that could be 
emitted each year to meet the five percent requirement. The ``Projected 
Annual PM10 Emissions with BACM Implementation (tons)'' 
values are the projected actual emissions between 2024 and 2026 
reflecting the implementation of control measures. The ``Excess Benefit 
= Total PM10 Emissions Reductions Minus Five Percent

reductions each year beyond the five percent requirement.
    The 2023 Five Percent Plan demonstrates compliance with the five 
percent reduction requirement by comparing the cumulative reductions 
against the total five percent reduction values each year and shows 
that the reductions exceed the five percent per year requirement. Most 
of the required reductions were achieved in the early years of the 
plan. The EPA encourages this approach as it accelerates the 
environmental benefits of the reductions.\43\ Because the 2023 Five 
Percent Plan demonstrates that the area will achieve the requisite 
reductions from 2024 until the modeled attainment date in 2026, the EPA 
proposes to find that Plan meets the CAA section 189(d) five percent 
requirement.

E. Reasonable Further Progress and Quantitative Milestones

    Pursuant to CAA sections 172(c)(2) and 189(c)(1), the State must 
demonstrate RFP in the 2023 Five Percent Plan. We have explained in 
guidance that for areas such as the West Pinal County PM10 
Nonattainment Area where ``the nonattainment problem is attributed to 
area type sources (e.g., fugitive dust, etc.), RFP should be met by 
showing annual incremental emission reductions sufficient generally to 
maintain linear progress towards attainment. Total PM10 
emissions should not remain constant or increase from 1 year to the 
next in such an area.'' \44\ Further, we have stated that, ``in 
reviewing the SIP, EPA will determine whether the annual incremental 
emission reductions to be achieved are reasonable in light of the 
statutory objective to ensure timely attainment of the PM10 
NAAQS.'' \45\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \44\ Addendum, 42015.
    \45\ Id. at 42016.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    CAA section 189(c) further requires PM10 attainment 
plans to contain quantitative milestones that are to be achieved every 
three years and that demonstrate RFP for the area. These quantitative 
milestones should consist of elements that allow RFP to be quantified 
or measured objectively. Specifically, States should identify and 
submit quantitative milestones that allow for evaluation of whether the 
plan is achieving emissions reductions adequate to attain the NAAQS by 
the applicable attainment date.\46\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \46\ Id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

F. Contingency Measures

    CAA section 172(c)(9) requires that attainment plans provide for 
the implementation of specific measures to be undertaken if the area 
fails to meet RFP requirements or fails to attain the PM10 
standard as projected in the plan. That section further requires that 
such measures are to take effect in any such case without further 
action by the State or the EPA. The CAA does not specify how many 
contingency measures are necessary nor does it specify the level of 
emission reductions they must achieve.
    The purpose of contingency measures is to continue progress in 
reducing emissions while a State revises its SIP to meet the missed RFP 
milestone or to develop a new plan demonstrating attainment of the 
NAAQS. Contingency measures must consist of measures that the State is 
not otherwise relying on to meet other attainment plan requirements in 
the area. Thus, these additional emission reductions that will be 
achieved by the contingency measures ensure continued progress towards 
attainment while the State is revising the SIP to correct the failure 
to meet RFP or to attain.
    In interpreting the requirement that the contingency measures must 
``take effect without further action by the State or the 
Administrator,'' the General Preamble provides the following general 
guidance: ``[s]tates must show that their contingency measures can be 
implemented with minimal further action on their part and with no 
additional rulemaking actions such as public hearings or legislative 
review.'' Further, ``[i]n general, EPA will expect all actions needed 
to affect full implementation of the measures to occur within 60 days 
after EPA notifies the State of its failure.''
    In December 2024, the EPA released the ``Guidance on the 
Preparation of State Implementation Plan Provisions that Address the 
Nonattainment Area Contingency Measure Requirements for Ozone and 
Particulate Matter (December 3, 2024)'' (``Revised Contingency Measure 
Guidance'').\49\ This guidance primarily relates to the EPA's 
recommendations concerning the specific amount of emissions reductions 
that implementation of contingency

[[Page 66056]]

measures should achieve and the timing for when the emissions 
reductions from the contingency measures should occur.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \49\ The EPA announced the availability of the guidance document 
at 89 FR 101602 (Dec. 16, 2024). A copy of the guidance document 
itself is available in the docket for this action. The EPA had 
previously released a draft of this document, ``Draft: Guidance on 
the Preparation of State Implementation Plan Provisions that Address 
the Nonattainment Area Contingency Measure Requirements for Ozone 
and Particulate Matter (DRAFT--3/17/23--Public Review Version)'' 
(``Draft Revised Contingency Measure Guidance''). The EPA published 
a notice of availability for the Draft Revised Contingency Measure 
Guidance at 88 FR 17571 (Mar. 23, 2023). The Revised Contingency 
Measure Guidance that the EPA finalized in December 2024 is 
consistent with the guidance set forth in the Draft Revised 
Contingency Measure Guidance that the EPA released in March 2023.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Prior to the release of the Revised Contingency Measure Guidance, 
the EPA's recommendation for the amount of emissions reductions to 
achieve from implementation of contingency measures was one year's 
worth of RFP. For PM10, prior EPA guidance recommended that 
RFP should represent generally linear progress towards attainment 
(i.e., the difference between the attainment projected inventory \50\ 
and the base year emissions inventory, divided by the number of years 
between the base year and the attainment year).\51\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \50\ The term ``attainment projected inventory'' is described 
further in Section 3.8.1 (for ozone) and Section 3.8.2 (for 
particulate matter) of the EPA's ``Emissions Inventory Guidance for 
Implementation of Ozone and Particulate Matter NAAQS and Regional 
Haze Regulations.'' See https://www.EPA.gov/air-emissions-inventories/air-emissions-inventory-guidance-implementation-ozone-and-particulate.
    \51\ 59 FR 41998, 42015 (Aug. 16, 1994).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The Revised Contingency Measure Guidance introduces ``one year's 
worth of progress,'' a metric intended to be more closely tied to the 
emissions reductions required for attainment of the NAAQS, for 
determining the amount of emissions reductions that contingency 
measures should achieve. One year's worth of ``progress'' is calculated 
by determining the average annual reductions between the base year 
emissions inventory and the projected attainment year emissions 
inventory, determining what percentage of the base year emissions 
inventory this amount represents, and then applying that percentage to 
the projected attainment year emissions inventory to determine the 
amount of reductions needed to ensure ongoing progress if contingency 
measures are triggered.\52\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \52\ See Chapter 3 of the Revised Contingency Measure Guidance.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The 2023 Five Percent Plan identified one adopted contingency 
measure of a speed limit reduction on public unpaved roads. This 
contingency measure is PCAQCD Rule 4-1-030.6.C, which the State 
submitted to the EPA for approval into the SIP on February 13, 2023. 
The measure would require owners or operators of unpaved public roads 
of 26 annual average daily traffic or more to establish a speed limit 
of 15 miles per hour in the event that the area fails to make RFP or 
fails to attain the PM10 NAAQS by the attainment date.\53\ 
The EPA is proposing to approve Rule 4-1-030.6.C in a separate notice 
in today's Federal Register. While that rulemaking action evaluates the 
approvability of the rule into the SIP, in this action we evaluate 
whether the contingency provision in that rule satisfies the 
contingency measure planning requirement for the PM10 NAAQS 
associated with the submitted plan.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \53\ 2023 Five Percent Plan, Chapter 9, Attainment 
Demonstration, pp. 9-28-9-29.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    If the EPA finalizes the measure's approval into the SIP, our 
analysis indicates that the measure meets all relevant requirements to 
satisfy the contingency measure requirement for the PM10 
NAAQS. The measure has been fully adopted and will be triggered upon an 
EPA finding that the area has failed to attain the NAAQS by the 
applicable attainment date or has failed to meet the RFP requirement. 
The measure goes into effect immediately upon such a finding, with no 
additional action required by the State. In addition, the method used 
to estimate emissions reductions from this contingency measure is 
consistent with the EPA's recommended calculation methods for such 
measures, and the total reductions exceed the target of one year's 
worth of progress.\54\ Because it meets all applicable requirements, 
the EPA proposes to approve the contingency measure element described 
in the 2023 Five Percent Plan.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \54\ As explained in the 2023 Five Percent Plan, the contingency 
measure is expected to generate 950.81 tons of reductions. The 
threshold for one year's worth of progress is 657 tons. Thus, the 
measure is sufficient to achieve the quantity of reductions 
indicated in the EPA's Revised Contingency Measure Guidance. The EPA 
notes that under the previously suggested method for calculating 
contingency measure reductions (one year's worth of RFP), the value 
would be 795 tons. The measure thus achieves sufficient reductions 
under both previous and current EPA guidance.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

G. Transportation Conformity and Motor Vehicle Emissions Budgets

    Actions involving Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) or Federal 
Transit Administration (FTA) funding or approval are subject to the 
EPA's transportation conformity rule, codified at 40 CFR part 93, 
subpart A. Under this rule, metropolitan planning organizations (MPOs) 
in nonattainment and maintenance areas coordinate with State and local 
air quality and transportation agencies, the EPA, the FHWA, and the FTA 
to determine that an area's regional transportation plans and 
transportation improvement programs conform to the applicable SIP. This 
determination typically includes a showing that estimated emissions 
from existing and planned highway and transit systems are less than or 
equal to the budgets that the EPA has found adequate or approved in the 
area's control strategy SIP.\55\ Budgets are generally established for 
specific years and specific pollutants or precursors. Attainment plans 
for PM10 nonattainment areas should identify budgets for on-
road mobile source emissions of PM10, i.e., vehicle 
emissions and fugitive dust emissions, in the area for each RFP 
milestone year, as appropriate, and the attainment year, if the plan 
demonstrates attainment.\56\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \55\ See definition of ``control strategy implementation plan 
revision'' at 40 CFR 93.101.
    \56\ 40 CFR 93.102(b)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For budgets to be approvable, they must meet, at a minimum, the 
EPA's adequacy criteria at 40 CFR 93.118(e)(4). While we have not yet 
made an adequacy finding, the EPA is starting the adequacy process with 
this notice and as such, the EPA is also proposing to approve the 
budgets based on these criteria. To meet these requirements, the 
budgets must be consistent with the attainment and RFP requirements and 
reflect all the motor vehicle control measures contained in the 
attainment and RFP demonstrations.\57\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \57\ 40 CFR 93.118(e)(4)(iii), (iv) and (v). For more 
information on the transportation conformity requirements and 
applicable policies on budgets, please visit our transportation 
conformity website at: https://www.epa.gov/state-and-local-transportation/transportation-conformity.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The EPA's process for determining the adequacy of a budget consists 
of three basic steps: (1) providing public notification of a SIP 
submission; (2) providing the public the opportunity to comment on the 
budget during a public comment period; and (3) making a finding of 
adequacy or inadequacy.\58\ During the comment period for this notice, 
the public can comment on the adequacy of the budgets in addition to 
other aspects of this proposed rule.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \58\ 40 CFR 93.118(f)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The 2023 Five Percent Plan specifies the maximum transportation-
related PM10 emissions for the RFP milestone year of 2023, 
and for the RFP milestone and attainment year of 2026. The State's 
submitted 2023 and 2026 budgets for PM10 are included in 
Table 4 of this document. These budgets include emissions from vehicle 
exhaust, tire wear, brake wear, road construction, re-entrained dust 
from vehicles traveling on paved roads, and fugitive dust generated 
from vehicles traveling on public unpaved and private non-agricultural 
\59\ unpaved roads.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \59\ Unpaved, private, non-agricultural roads have been included 
as an emission source category in the motor vehicle emissions 
budgets as they are generally accessible and used by the public. 
Conversely, unpaved, private, agricultural roads are primarily used 
to access irrigation canals or farm fields and are not included as a 
category in the motor vehicle emissions budgets because they are not 
generally accessed or used by the public.

estimating fugitive PM10 emissions were interpolated from 
the 2017 base year VMT.\65\ Unpaved private non-agricultural VMT 
estimates for estimating fugitive PM10 were held constant 
from the 2017 base year VMT estimates.\66\

    We are proposing to approve the budgets for 2023 and 2026 as part 
of our approval of the 2023 Five Percent Plan. The EPA has determined 
that the 2023 and 2026 motor vehicle emissions budgets are consistent 
with emission control measures in the SIP and the attainment 
demonstration, five percent demonstration, and RFP demonstration. The 
details of the EPA's evaluation of the budgets for compliance with the 
budget adequacy criteria of 40 CFR 93.118(e) is provided in a separate 
document included in the docket for this rulemaking.\67\ If we find the 
budgets adequate or finalize approval of the budgets in the 2023 Five 
Percent Plan as proposed, then these budgets must be used in future 
transportation conformity analyses for the West Pinal County 
PM10 Nonattainment Area.\68\

H. Adequate Legal Authority

    CAA section 110(a)(2)(E)(i) requires that implementation plans 
provide necessary assurances that the State (or the local government in 
the case of delegation) will have adequate personnel, funding and 
authority under State law. Requirements for legal authority are further 
defined in 40 CFR part 51, subpart L (sections 51.230-51.232) and for 
resources in 40 CFR 51.280.
    States and responsible local agencies must demonstrate that they 
have the legal authority to adopt and enforce provisions of the SIP and 
to obtain information necessary to determine compliance. These 
requirements are addressed in the cover letters and submittal package 
for the 2023 Five Percent Plan.\69\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \69\ Letter dated December 13, 2023, from Hether Krause, Deputy 
Director, Air Quality Division, ADEQ, to Martha Guzman, Regional 
Administrator, EPA Region IX, Subject: ``Arizona State 
Implementation Plan Revision, Maricopa Association of Governments 
2023 Five Percent Particulate Plan for PM-10 For the West Pinal 
County Nonattainment Area.''
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    MAG derives its authority to develop and adopt air quality plans, 
including the 2023 Five Percent Plan, from Arizona Revised Statute 
(ARS) 49-406 and from a June 22, 2016 letter from the Governor of 
Arizona designating MAG as responsible for those tasks.\70\ ADEQ is 
authorized to adopt and submit the 2023 Five Percent Plan by ARS 49-404 
and ARS 49-406. PCAQCD implements air quality programs within Pinal 
County.

    For the reasons discussed above, we propose to find that the 
requirements of CAA section 110(a)(2)(E) and related regulations have 
been met with respect to legal authority.

V. Summary of Proposed Actions

    The EPA is proposing to approve the CAA section 189(d) plan for the 
West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area as meeting all 
relevant Moderate, Serious, and CAA section 189(d) requirements. 
Specifically, we propose to approve the following:
    (1) The 2017 baseline emissions inventory and the attainment year 
emission inventories as meeting the requirements of CAA section 
172(c)(3);

[[Page 66058]]

    (2) the BACM demonstration as meeting the requirements of CAA 
section 189(b)(1)(B), and the RACM demonstration as meeting the 
requirements of CAA sections 189(a)(1)(C) and 172(c)(1);
    (3) the attainment demonstration as meeting the requirements of CAA 
sections 189(d) and 179(d)(3), with an attainment date of December 31, 
2026;
    (4) the five percent demonstration as meeting the requirements of 
CAA section 189(d);
    (5) the reasonable further progress and quantitative milestone 
demonstrations as meeting the requirements of CAA sections 172(c)(2) 
and 189(c);
    (6) the contingency measure as meeting the requirements of CAA 
section 172(c)(9); and
    (7) the motor vehicle emissions budgets, as they meet the criteria 
for budgets in CAA section 176(c) and 40 CFR 93.118(e)(4).
    The EPA is also starting the adequacy process for these budgets.

VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews

    Under the CAA, the Administrator is required to approve a SIP 
submission that complies with the provisions of the Act and applicable 
Federal regulations. 42 U.S.C. 7410(k); 40 CFR 52.02(a). Thus, in 
reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA's role is to approve State choices, 
provided that they meet the criteria of the CAA. Accordingly, this 
proposed action merely proposes to approve State law as meeting Federal 
requirements and does not impose additional requirements beyond those 
imposed by State law. For that reason, this proposed action:
     Is not a significant regulatory action subject to review 
by the Office of Management and Budget under Executive Order 12866 (58 
FR 51735, Oct. 4, 1993);
     Is not an Executive Order 14192 (90 FR 9065, Feb. 6, 2025) 
regulatory action because this action is not significant under 
Executive Order 12866;
     Does not impose an information collection burden under the 
provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq.);
     Is certified as not having a significant economic impact 
on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory 
Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.);
     Does not contain any unfunded mandate or significantly or 
uniquely affect small governments, as described in the Unfunded 
Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (Pub. L. 104-4);
     Does not have federalism implications as specified in 
Executive Order 13132 (64 FR 43255, Aug. 10, 1999);
     Is not subject to Executive Order 13045 (62 FR 19885, Apr. 
23, 1997) because it proposes to approve a State program;
     Is not a significant regulatory action subject to 
Executive Order 13211 (66 FR 28355, May 22, 2001); and
     Is not subject to requirements of section 12(d) of the 
National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (15 U.S.C. 272 
note) because application of those requirements would be inconsistent 
with the CAA.
    In addition, the SIP is not approved to apply on any Indian 
reservation land or in any other area where the EPA or an Indian Tribe 
has demonstrated that a Tribe has jurisdiction. In those areas of 
Indian country, the rule does not have Tribal implications and will not 
impose substantial direct costs on Tribal governments or preempt Tribal 
law as specified by Executive Order 13175 (65 FR 67249, Nov. 9, 2000).
